--- title: "Reading & Writing Data" subtitle: "≈ readr · readxl · arrow · DBI" jupyter: python3 --- Import is where silent damage happens: a column typed wrong, a missing marker read as text, a Thai name decoded as noise. This chapter covers which formats remember dtypes, how CSV inference fails, Thai legacy encodings, Parquet and IPC as the bridge to R, Excel, SQLite, and folders of files. Lazy scans, pushdown and hive partitions are in [Lazy API](lazy.qmd#sec-lazy-sources); one-line translations are in the [cheatsheet](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-io). ## In tidyverse {#sec-io-tidyverse} ```r library(tidyverse); library(readxl); library(arrow); library(DBI) weather <- read_csv("weather.csv") # "NA" missing, dates parsed problems(weather) # what failed to parse ris <- read_csv("ris_export.csv", col_types = cols(hn = col_character()), locale = locale(encoding = "TIS-620", tz = "Asia/Bangkok")) read_excel("exams.xlsx", sheet = "CT", skip = 2) write_parquet(exams, "exams.parquet"); read_feather("exams.arrow") con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "ris.sqlite") dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM exams WHERE hn = ?", params = list("0012345")) dbWriteTable(con, "exams", exams) read_csv(files, id = "path") # many files, one frame ``` readr is generous: R4DS 2e describes it guessing each column from 1,000 rows spaced evenly through the file, reading `""` and `"NA"` as missing, parsing dates, and logging failures for `problems()`. Polars' CSV reader is literal: it guesses from the **first 100 rows**, `"NA"` is a string, dates stay strings, and a value that doesn't fit the guess is an error. ## Mental model {#sec-io-model} ```text EAGER: a DataFrame now LAZY: a plan (Lazy API chapter) ─────────── ───────────────────────────────── ───────────────────────────────── read pl.read_csv pl.read_parquet pl.scan_csv pl.scan_parquet pl.read_ipc pl.read_ndjson pl.scan_ipc pl.scan_ndjson pl.read_excel pl.read_database (none: Excel and SQL are eager only) write df.write_csv df.write_parquet lf.sink_csv lf.sink_parquet df.write_ipc df.write_ndjson lf.sink_ipc lf.sink_ndjson df.write_excel df.write_database What a file remembers about dtypes Parquet, IPC the whole Polars schema ──► read back exactly NDJSON numbers, booleans, lists, structs; the rest becomes text Excel numbers, booleans, dates; the rest becomes text CSV nothing: every value is text, re-guessed on every read ``` The working rule: **CSV and Excel are for exchange, Parquet is for storage.** Parse a CSV carefully once, then keep the typed result as Parquet. ## Mechanics {#sec-io-mechanics} Every file below goes into a temporary directory deleted at the end. ::: {#7c6e14fb .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import datetime as dt import importlib.util import io import sqlite3 import tempfile from functools import partial from pathlib import Path import polars as pl import xlsxwriter from pl_notes import datasets tmp = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() data_dir = Path(tmp.name) ``` ::: ### Which formats keep dtypes {#sec-io-dtypes} An invented exam log with the dtypes that usually go wrong: ::: {#9ce13fd4 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} exams_df = pl.DataFrame({ "hn": ["0012345", "0098765", "0012345"], "modality": ["CT", "MR", "XR"], "arrived": [dt.datetime(2024, 1, 15, 8, 30), dt.datetime(2024, 1, 15, 9, 5), dt.datetime(2024, 1, 16, 14, 0)], "exam_date": [dt.date(2024, 1, 15), dt.date(2024, 1, 15), dt.date(2024, 1, 16)], "tat_min": [35.5, None, 12.0], "n_images": [120, 300, 2], "cost": ["1500.50", "8200.00", "350.00"], "findings": [["nodule"], [], ["fracture", "effusion"]], }).with_columns( pl.col("modality").cast(pl.Enum(["XR", "CT", "MR"])), pl.col("arrived").dt.replace_time_zone("Asia/Bangkok"), pl.col("n_images").cast(pl.UInt16), pl.col("cost").cast(pl.Decimal(10, 2)), ) exams_df ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Write each column to each format, read it back, and record the dtype that came back (`✓` = unchanged): ::: {#0267b055 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} formats = { "parquet": (pl.DataFrame.write_parquet, pl.read_parquet), "ipc": (pl.DataFrame.write_ipc, pl.read_ipc), "csv": (pl.DataFrame.write_csv, pl.read_csv), "ndjson": (pl.DataFrame.write_ndjson, pl.read_ndjson), "xlsx": (pl.DataFrame.write_excel, pl.read_excel), } def roundtrip(column: str, fmt: str) -> str: write, read = formats[fmt] path = data_dir / f"roundtrip.{fmt}" try: write(exams_df.select(column), path) except Exception as err: return f"✗ {type(err).__name__}" dtype = read(path).schema[column] return "✓" if dtype == exams_df.schema[column] else str(dtype) pl.DataFrame( {"column": exams_df.columns} | {fmt: [roundtrip(c, fmt) for c in exams_df.columns] for fmt in formats} ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Parquet and IPC store the Arrow schema in the file, so the Enum levels, the zone, the unsigned width and the decimal scale all survive. CSV turns `hn` into `12345`, as readr would (both guess a number). Excel refuses a zoned datetime and CSV refuses a list. ### CSV: type inference {#sec-io-csv-infer} `pl_notes.datasets` reads `weather.csv` with `infer_schema_length=None` for a reason. Locate the file the way `datasets.py` does (without importing the package) and read it with only the `"NA"` fix: ::: {#20dca1f6 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} nyc_spec = importlib.util.find_spec("nycflights13") weather_path = Path(next(iter(nyc_spec.submodule_search_locations))) / "data" / "weather.csv" ``` ::: ::: {#aa9023d6 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.read_csv(weather_path, null_values="NA") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
ComputeError: could not parse `0.05` as dtype `i64` at column 'precip' (column number 12)

The current offset in the file is 22099 bytes.

You might want to try:
- increasing `infer_schema_length` (e.g. `infer_schema_length=10000`),
- increasing `infer_schema_files` (e.g. `infer_schema_files=50`),
- specifying correct dtype with the `schema_overrides` argument
- setting `ignore_errors` to `True`,
- adding `0.05` to the `null_values` list.

Original error: ```invalid primitive value found during CSV parsing```
``` ::: ::: ::: `precip` is `0` in rows 0–254 and `0.05` in row 255, so 100 rows of zeros said `Int64`. Fixing that column alone moves the error to `visib`, whose first fraction is in row 258: ::: {#552ecd8a .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.read_csv(weather_path, null_values="NA", schema_overrides={"precip": pl.Float64}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
ComputeError: could not parse `2.5` as dtype `i64` at column 'visib' (column number 14)

The current offset in the file is 22344 bytes.

You might want to try:
- increasing `infer_schema_length` (e.g. `infer_schema_length=10000`),
- increasing `infer_schema_files` (e.g. `infer_schema_files=50`),
- specifying correct dtype with the `schema_overrides` argument
- setting `ignore_errors` to `True`,
- adding `2.5` to the `null_values` list.

Original error: ```invalid primitive value found during CSV parsing```
``` ::: ::: ::: Name both, or let inference see every row (the docstring warns that `None` is slow on big files; `10_000` is a middle ground): ::: {#ce2c04a4 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df = pl.read_csv( weather_path, null_values="NA", schema_overrides={"precip": pl.Float64, "visib": pl.Float64} ) weather_df.equals(pl.read_csv(weather_path, null_values="NA", infer_schema_length=None)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` True ``` ::: ::: The error message's fourth suggestion, `ignore_errors=True`, is the one to refuse: ::: {#73ad8ede .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df_ignored = pl.read_csv(weather_path, null_values="NA", ignore_errors=True) weather_df_ignored.select(pl.col("precip", "visib").null_count()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

shape: (2, 2)

``` ::: ::: The row-level version (which values failed) is a [Data Model recipe](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-recipes). | Argument | Columns | Inference | Note | |---|---|---|---| | `schema={...}` | all | none | matched **by name** in 2.0: a name missing from the header, or a header name missing from `schema`, raises `SchemaError` | | `schema_overrides={...}` | some | for the rest | a misspelled name is **silently ignored** | | `infer_schema=False` | all `String` | none | ≈ `col_types = cols(.default = "c")` | | `infer_schema_length=n` | all | first *n* rows; `None` = all | ≈ `guess_max` | | `new_columns=`, `with_column_names=fn` | renames | — | ≈ `col_names = c(...)`, `name_repair = fn` | : Controlling dtypes {.striped} ### CSV: nulls, dates, dialect {#sec-io-csv-dialect} An invented RIS export with the usual problems: hospital numbers with leading zeros, `-99` for "not recorded", Buddhist-era dates written day-first, and naive timestamps. Read plainly, `hn` becomes `12345`, `-99` a real dose, and both date columns strings: ::: {#72ccd3a8 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} ris_csv = """hn,name,exam_date,arrived,dlp 0012345,สมชาย ใจดี,15/01/2567,2024-01-15 08:30:00,512.4 0098765,มาลี สุขใจ,01/02/2567,2024-02-01 14:05:00,-99 """.encode() ris_df = pl.read_csv( ris_csv, schema_overrides={"hn": pl.String}, null_values={"dlp": "-99"}, # per column: {name: one string} try_parse_dates=True, ) ris_df ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 5)

"0098765""มาลี สุขใจ"2567-02-012024-02-01 14:05:00null
``` ::: ::: `try_parse_dates` read `01/02/2567` as **1 February**: slashes are taken day-first, which suits Thai data and misreads American data. It also accepts the year 2567. Buddhist-era years run 543 ahead: ::: {#6290ae89 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} ris_df.with_columns( pl.col("exam_date").dt.offset_by("-543y"), pl.col("arrived").dt.replace_time_zone("Asia/Bangkok"), # see @sec-io-tz-trap ).select("hn", "exam_date", "arrived") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}

One pattern is chosen per column from the inference rows, so a US date such as `02/15/2024` inside them leaves the column a string, and after them raises. Numbers have a similar edge: `NaN`, `inf` and `-inf` parse as floats, lowercase `nan` turns the column into a string. The rest of the dialect, on a semicolon export with title lines, a comment and decimal commas: ::: {#859e1fdd .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} workload_csv = """Radiology workload report Exported from RIS modality;n_exams;mean_dlp # CT includes PET-CT CT;1204;512,4 MR;388; """.encode() pl.read_csv(workload_csv, skip_lines=2, separator=";", comment_prefix="#", decimal_comma=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: | readr | Polars | Note | |---|---|---| | `skip = 2` | `skip_rows=2` / `skip_lines=2` | CSV rows (a quoted field may span lines) / raw lines | | `comment = "#"`, `locale(decimal_mark = ",")` | `comment_prefix="#"`, `decimal_comma=True` | | | `na = c("", "NA")` | `null_values=[...]` or `{col: str}` | `""` is null by default, a quoted `""` stays an empty string | | duplicate names → `a...1`, `a...2` | `a`, `a_duplicated_0` | | : Dialect options beyond the cheatsheet {.striped} A row with too few fields is padded with nulls; one with too many raises unless `truncate_ragged_lines=True`. Windows line endings and a UTF-8 BOM (Excel's "CSV UTF-8") need no options. ### CSV: Thai legacy encodings {#sec-io-encoding} Older Thai Windows systems export TIS-620 / cp874, one byte per Thai character. Polars parses only UTF-8: ::: {#be7921da .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} patients_text = "hn,name,ward\n0012345,สมชาย ใจดี,อายุรกรรม\n0098765,มาลี สุขใจ,ศัลยกรรม\n" legacy_path = data_dir / "patients_cp874.csv" _ = legacy_path.write_bytes(patients_text.encode("cp874")) # what the old export looks like ``` ::: ::: {#34cc3aab .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.read_csv(legacy_path) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
ComputeError: invalid utf-8 sequence
``` ::: ::: ::: In 2.0, eager `read_csv()` accepts any Python codec name (`"cp874"`, `"tis-620"`, `"iso8859_11"`; not `"windows-874"`): it decodes the whole file in Python, re-encodes it as UTF-8 in memory, then parses. `scan_csv()` streams and can't: it raises `ValueError` for anything but `"utf8"` and `"utf8-lossy"`. ::: {#fd9283ea .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.read_csv(legacy_path, encoding="cp874", schema_overrides={"hn": pl.String}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: `"utf8-lossy"` replaces each byte sequence that isn't valid UTF-8 with `�` and keeps going: ::: {#e8f24c55 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.read_csv(legacy_path, encoding="utf8-lossy", schema_overrides={"hn": pl.String}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ```{=html}

And `㨴` is not a `�`: the cp874 bytes of `ใจด` (`E3 A8 B4`) happen to be valid UTF-8, so counting `�` undercounts the damage. readr has `guess_encoding()`; Polars has no detector, so know the source system. ### CSV: writing {#sec-io-csv-write} ::: {#a354ed8e .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} report_df = pl.DataFrame({ "hn": ["0012345", "0098765"], "name": ["ใจดี, สมชาย", 'Mali "M" S'], "dlp": [0.1 + 0.2, 1e-7], "n_series": [3, None], "arrived": [dt.datetime(2024, 1, 15, 8, 30), dt.datetime(2024, 1, 15, 9, 5)], }).with_columns(pl.col("arrived").dt.replace_time_zone("Asia/Bangkok")) print(report_df.write_csv()) # no path: returns the text ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` hn,name,dlp,n_series,arrived 0012345,"ใจดี, สมชาย",0.30000000000000004,3,2024-01-15T08:30:00.000000+0700 0098765,"Mali ""M"" S",1e-7,,2024-01-15T09:05:00.000000+0700 ``` ::: ::: Floats get every digit needed to read them back exactly, null is an empty field, quotes appear only where needed, and a zoned datetime keeps its offset (`+0700`) but not its zone name: `try_parse_dates=True` reads it back as UTC. The options: ::: {#3c24d335 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(report_df.write_csv( null_value="NA", float_precision=3, # fixed decimals: 1e-7 becomes 0.000 datetime_format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M", # the offset is gone too quote_style="non_numeric", )) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` "hn","name","dlp","n_series","arrived" "0012345","ใจดี, สมชาย",0.300,3,"2024-01-15 08:30" "0098765","Mali ""M"" S",0.000,NA,"2024-01-15 09:05" ``` ::: ::: | readr | Polars `write_csv()` | Note | |---|---|---| | `na = "NA"` (default) | `null_value="NA"` | Polars' default is an empty field | | `quote = "needed"` / `"all"` / `"none"` | `quote_style="necessary"` / `"always"` / `"never"` | plus `"non_numeric"`; `"never"` breaks `ใจดี, สมชาย` into two fields | | `write_excel_csv()` | `include_bom=True` | the BOM tells Excel the file is UTF-8, so Thai displays | | `write_csv(df, "f.csv.gz")` | `compression="gzip"` or `"zstd"` | the path must end in `.gz`, or `check_extension=False` | : Writing CSV {.striped} `Duration`, `List`, `Struct` and `Array` columns can't be written to CSV (`ComputeError`). ### Parquet {#sec-io-parquet} The same `flights` table in each format, written to memory (the sizes are reproducible): ::: {#b82b2576 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df = datasets.flights() writers = { "csv": flights_df.write_csv, "csv, gzip": partial(flights_df.write_csv, compression="gzip"), "ndjson": flights_df.write_ndjson, "ipc": flights_df.write_ipc, "ipc, zstd": partial(flights_df.write_ipc, compression="zstd"), "parquet, uncompressed": partial(flights_df.write_parquet, compression="uncompressed"), "parquet, snappy": partial(flights_df.write_parquet, compression="snappy"), "parquet, zstd": flights_df.write_parquet, } def size_mb(write) -> float: buffer = io.BytesIO() write(buffer) return round(buffer.getbuffer().nbytes / 1e6, 1) pl.DataFrame({"format": list(writers), "MB": [size_mb(w) for w in writers.values()]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Uncompressed Parquet is already a sixth of the CSV: each column is stored separately and dictionary/run-length encoded (`RLE_DICTIONARY`), so repeated carriers, airports and years cost almost nothing. The codec matters less: `zstd` is the default (`compression_level=` 1–22, default 3); `gzip` and `brotli` land within 5% of it, and `snappy` is for old readers. Read part of a file, its schema, or its key-value metadata without the data. `write_parquet(metadata=)` stores strings in the file footer, a good place for provenance: ::: {#28ceb9bd .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} exams_path = data_dir / "exams.parquet" exams_df.write_parquet(exams_path, metadata={"source": "RIS export", "exported": "2024-02-01"}) print(pl.read_parquet(exams_path, columns=["hn", "modality"], n_rows=1)) print(pl.read_parquet_schema(exams_path)["arrived"]) {k: v for k, v in pl.read_parquet_metadata(exams_path).items() if k != "ARROW:schema"} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` shape: (1, 2) ┌─────────┬──────────┐ │ hn ┆ modality │ │ --- ┆ --- │ │ str ┆ enum │ ╞═════════╪══════════╡ │ 0012345 ┆ CT │ └─────────┴──────────┘ Datetime(time_unit='us', time_zone='Asia/Bangkok') ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ``` {'exported': '2024-02-01', 'source': 'RIS export'} ``` ::: ::: Two layout options pay off at read time. `row_group_size=` sets rows per row group, the unit a reader can skip; `statistics=True` (the default) writes each row group's min, max and null count per column (`"full"` adds distinct counts). A filtered `scan_parquet()` skips row groups whose statistics rule them out ([Lazy API](lazy.qmd#sec-lazy-sources)), so sort by a common filter column before writing. **The bridge to R.** Polars writes standard Arrow types. What the file holds was checked with `pyarrow` against a Polars-written file; the R column follows arrow's documented type mapping (R not run here): | Polars dtype | Arrow type in the file | `arrow::read_parquet()` in R | |---|---|---| | `Enum` | dictionary, `ordered=True` | factor | | `Categorical` | dictionary | factor | | `Datetime("us", "Asia/Bangkok")` | `timestamp[us, tz=Asia/Bangkok]` | POSIXct in that zone | | `Date` | `date32` | `Date` | | `Decimal(10, 2)` | `decimal128(10, 2)` | double | | `List(String)`, `Struct` | `large_list`, `struct` | list-column, data-frame column | : Polars → Parquet → R {.striped} The way back loses one thing. An Arrow dictionary without Polars' own field metadata, which is what R's arrow writes for a factor, reads as `Categorical`, even when ordered. Restore the levels with `cast(pl.Enum([...]))`. ### IPC / Feather {#sec-io-ipc} Arrow IPC is the in-memory layout written to disk: fast, and large unless compressed (62 MB vs 6.9 MB above). Feather v2 *is* the IPC file format, so R reads it with `arrow::read_feather()`: ::: {#7f8836e8 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} exams_ipc = data_dir / "exams.arrow" exams_df.write_ipc(exams_ipc, compression="zstd") # or "lz4"; default "uncompressed" exams_ipc.read_bytes()[:6], pl.read_ipc(exams_ipc).equals(exams_df) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ``` (b'ARROW1', True) ``` ::: ::: Polars writes the newest Arrow types by default (strings as `string_view`); for an older Arrow reader pass `compat_level=pl.CompatLevel.oldest()`, which writes `large_string`. Parquet for archives and exchange, IPC for short-lived handoffs. ### NDJSON and JSON {#sec-io-json} ::: {#4c78e0d0 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} exams_json = exams_df.select("hn", "exam_date", "findings").head(2).write_ndjson() print(exams_json) pl.read_ndjson(exams_json.encode(), schema_overrides={"exam_date": pl.Date}).schema ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` {"hn":"0012345","exam_date":"2024-01-15","findings":["nodule"]} {"hn":"0098765","exam_date":"2024-01-15","findings":[]} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ``` Schema([('hn', String), ('exam_date', Date), ('findings', List(String))]) ``` ::: ::: One object per line: lists and structs survive, dates return as strings unless overridden. `write_json()` writes one array of row objects instead. Rectangling arbitrary JSON is in [Nested Data](../types/nested.qmd). ### Excel {#sec-io-excel} `write_excel()` writes through `xlsxwriter`. For several sheets (≈ `writexl::write_xlsx(list(a = df1, b = df2))`), open the workbook yourself and pass it in. Excel has no time zones (a zoned column raises `TypeError`) and no lists, so flatten first: ::: {#3dc2223a .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} exams_xlsx = data_dir / "exams.xlsx" exams_df_flat = exams_df.with_columns( pl.col("arrived").dt.replace_time_zone(None), pl.col("findings").list.join("; "), ) with xlsxwriter.Workbook(exams_xlsx) as workbook: for (day,), exams_df_day in exams_df_flat.partition_by("exam_date", as_dict=True).items(): exams_df_day.write_excel(workbook, worksheet=str(day)) exams_df_flat.write_excel( workbook, worksheet="ทั้งหมด", # "all" autofit=True, freeze_panes="A2", # keep the header visible dtype_formats={pl.Datetime: "dd/mm/yyyy hh:mm"}, ) {name: sheet_df.shape for name, sheet_df in pl.read_excel(exams_xlsx, sheet_id=0).items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ``` {'2024-01-15': (2, 8), '2024-01-16': (1, 8), 'ทั้งหมด': (3, 8)} ``` ::: ::: `sheet_id=0` reads every sheet into a `{name: DataFrame}` dict; `sheet_name=` or `sheet_id=` (1-based) picks one, and the default is the first. Formats change what a cell **displays**, not what it stores; `float_precision=` (default 3) is a display format too. On the way back (@sec-io-dtypes), `hn` stays text because it was written as text. Excel stores every number as a double and Polars turns whole-number columns back into `Int64`, so `n_images` loses its `UInt16`; datetimes return in milliseconds. The readxl arguments map as below; `read_options` goes to the default `calamine` engine (via `fastexcel`) and handles title rows above the header: | readxl | `pl.read_excel()` | |---|---| | `sheet = "CT"`, `excel_sheets()` | `sheet_name="CT"`, `sheet_id=0` (all, as a dict) | | `skip = 2` | `read_options={"header_row": 2}` (0-based row of the header) | | `range = cell_cols("A:C")` | `read_options={"use_columns": "A:C"}` or `columns=[...]` | | `col_types = ...` | `schema_overrides={...}` | | `guess_max = 1000` (default) | `infer_schema_length=100` (default) | | `na = c("", "NA")` | in a numeric column, `""`, `NA`, `N/A`, `n/a`, `#N/A`, `NULL` read as null; in a text column they stay text | : readxl → Polars {.striped} The difference in guess windows matters more for Excel than for CSV (@sec-io-excel-trap). ### Databases {#sec-io-db} `pl.read_database()` takes a SQL string and any DB-API connection, including the standard library's `sqlite3`. `write_database()` does not: it needs a SQLAlchemy or ADBC connection (or a URI for one), and neither is installed here. ::: {#708198c9 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:") exams_df.select("hn", "exam_date").write_database("exams", con) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
TypeError: unrecognised connection type 'sqlite3.Connection'
``` ::: ::: ::: The standard-library route is `executemany()` over `iter_rows()`, with dates cast to ISO strings first (SQLite has no date type, and Python's implicit date adapter is deprecated since 3.12): ::: {#1bdbc395 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} con.execute( "CREATE TABLE exams (hn TEXT, modality TEXT, exam_date TEXT, tat_min REAL, n_images INTEGER)" ) exams_df_db = exams_df.select("hn", "modality", "exam_date", "tat_min", "n_images").with_columns( pl.col("modality", "exam_date").cast(pl.String) ) con.executemany("INSERT INTO exams VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", exams_df_db.iter_rows()) pl.read_database( "SELECT * FROM exams WHERE hn = ?", con, execute_options={"parameters": ["0012345"]}, # placeholders, never f-strings schema_overrides={"n_images": pl.Int32}, ).with_columns(pl.col("exam_date").str.to_date()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ```{=html}

Parse afterwards, as above. A SQLite query that returns no rows gives all-`Null` columns (no declared type to fall back on), and `iter_batches=True` needs `batch_size=`. | DBI | Polars | Requires | |---|---|---| | `dbGetQuery(con, sql, params = )` | `pl.read_database(sql, con, execute_options={"parameters": ...})` | a DB-API connection, SQLAlchemy, or ADBC | | `dbSendQuery()` + `dbFetch(n = )` | `read_database(..., iter_batches=True, batch_size=n)` | | | `dbGetQuery()` on a server database | `pl.read_database_uri(sql, "postgresql://…")` | `connectorx` (default) or ADBC | | `dbWriteTable()` | `df.write_database(name, connection, if_table_exists=)` | SQLAlchemy or ADBC | | dbplyr `tbl()` | none: send SQL, or load and go [lazy](lazy.qmd) | | : DBI → Polars {.striped} ### Many files and cloud storage {#sec-io-many} Four monthly exports; March gained a column, April reordered its columns: ::: {#696f1634 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} exports_dir = data_dir / "exports" exports_dir.mkdir() exports = { "2024-01": "accession,modality,tat_min\nA1,CT,35\nA2,MR,50\n", "2024-02": "accession,modality,tat_min\nB1,XR,12.5\n", "2024-03": "accession,modality,tat_min,radiologist\nC1,CT,40,Dr. A\n", "2024-04": "accession,tat_min,modality\nD1,22,US\n", } for month, text in exports.items(): (exports_dir / f"exams_{month}.csv").write_text(text) ``` ::: A glob reads matching files as one table. Inference spans files (`infer_schema_files=10`), so January's integers and February's float agree on `Float64`; `include_file_paths=` adds the source (≈ `read_csv(files, id = )`); `missing_columns="insert"` (unstable) fills a column some files lack: ::: {#784ec049 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.read_csv( exports_dir / "exams_2024-0[1-3].csv", include_file_paths="path", missing_columns="insert" ).with_columns(month=pl.col("path").str.extract(r"(\d{4}-\d{2})")).drop("path") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: When files disagree, read them one by one and stack with `how="diagonal_relaxed"`: columns matched by name, missing ones filled with null, dtypes widened (@sec-io-recipes). **Cloud storage** (described, not run). The readers and writers also take `s3://`, `gs://`, `az://` and `hf://` paths; the docstrings list AWS, GCP, Azure and Hugging Face. Credentials go in `storage_options={...}` (keys such as `"aws_region"`); without it, Polars looks in environment variables. Use `scan_parquet()` on cloud data so pushdown limits what is downloaded. ## Where it bites {#sec-io-gotchas} | readr / readxl / DBI | Polars | |---|---| | guesses from 1,000 rows | CSV and Excel guess from the first **100** | | a parse failure → `NA` + `problems()` | CSV raises; `ignore_errors=True` nulls silently (@sec-io-csv-infer) | | `"NA"` is missing | a string unless `null_values="NA"` ([Missing Values](../types/missing.qmd#sec-na-nan)) | | dates parsed by default | strings unless `try_parse_dates=True`; slashes day-first; any year accepted | | `locale(tz = )` places naive times in that zone | a zoned dtype in `schema_overrides` reads naive times as **UTC** (@sec-io-tz-trap) | | readxl: text in a numeric column → `NA` + warning | past the guess window: null, no warning, maybe a lost row (@sec-io-excel-trap) | | `locale(encoding = )` works everywhere | only eager `read_csv()` decodes non-UTF-8; `utf8-lossy` destroys Thai | | `write_csv()` writes `NA` for missing | an empty field; `float_precision=` can write `0.000` | | `dbWriteTable()` on any connection | `write_database()` needs SQLAlchemy or ADBC | : The differences at a glance {.striped} ### Excel: values past the guess window vanish {#sec-io-excel-trap} CSV raises when a later value breaks the guess. Excel doesn't. A dose column with 120 numbers, then 30 cells of text: ::: {#3bf750d2 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} doses_xlsx = data_dir / "doses.xlsx" with xlsxwriter.Workbook(doses_xlsx) as workbook: sheet = workbook.add_worksheet() sheet.write(0, 0, "dose_mg") for row in range(150): sheet.write(row + 1, 0, 1.5 if row < 120 else "pending") doses_df = pl.read_excel(doses_xlsx) doses_df_full = pl.read_excel(doses_xlsx, infer_schema_length=None) { "default": (doses_df.height, doses_df.schema["dose_mg"], doses_df["dose_mg"][-1]), "infer_schema_length=None": ( doses_df_full.height, doses_df_full.schema["dose_mg"], doses_df_full["dose_mg"][-1] ), } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=30} ``` {'default': (120, Float64, 1.5), 'infer_schema_length=None': (150, String, 'pending')} ``` ::: ::: With the default 100-row sample the column is `Float64`, each `"pending"` becomes null, and because those rows are then entirely null, `drop_empty_rows=True` (the default) deletes them: 150 rows in the sheet, 120 in the frame, no warning. `read_options={"dtype_coercion": "strict"}` doesn't help; it checks only the sampled rows. (Mixed cells *inside* the sample make the whole column `String`.) For any sheet a person typed into, pass `infer_schema_length=None` or `schema_overrides`, and check `height`. ### A naive timestamp read into a zone is taken as UTC {#sec-io-tz-trap} ::: {#b8457ecb .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} arrived_csv = b"arrived\n2024-01-15 08:30:00\n" pl.concat([ pl.read_csv(arrived_csv, schema_overrides={"arrived": pl.Datetime("us", "Asia/Bangkok")}), pl.read_csv(arrived_csv, try_parse_dates=True) .with_columns(pl.col("arrived").dt.replace_time_zone("Asia/Bangkok")), ]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=31} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 1)
arrived
datetime[μs, Asia/Bangkok]
2024-01-15 15:30:00 +07
2024-01-15 08:30:00 +07
``` ::: ::: Same string, seven hours apart. The reader treats a naive string as UTC and *converts* it to the zone; `replace_time_zone()` (like `str.to_datetime(time_zone=)`) *attaches* the zone to the wall-clock time, as readr's `locale(tz = )` does. Read naive, then attach ([Dates, Times & Durations](../types/datetime.qmd#sec-dt-tz)). ## Recipes {#sec-io-recipes} **A folder of monthly exports, month from the file name** (≈ `files |> set_names() |> map(read_csv) |> list_rbind(names_to = "file")`).
